qs.q: In diabetic ketoacidosis, the predominant ketone body measured by nitroprusside test is ---
qs.e: The nitroprusside test primarily detects acetoacetate among ketone bodies.

qs.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) but NOT diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)?

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Diabetic ketoacidosis is an acute, life‑threatening complication of insulin deficiency that produces hyperglycaemia, metabolic acidosis and ketonuria. Rapid recognition and treatment with fluids, insulin and electrolytes saves lives.

sections.p: DKA is defined by hyperglycaemia (>200 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L) and ketonemia/ketonuria. The presence of anion gap >12 mmol/L supports the diagnosis.
The American Diabetes Association stages DKA into mild, moderate and severe based on pH, bicarbonate and mental status. Severe DKA (pH <7.0) carries the highest mortality.

The leading trigger is insulin omission. Infections, especially urinary tract or pneumonia, are common precipitants. In low‑resource settings, malaria, TB, HIV and herbal remedies can also precipitate DKA.
Patients often report nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and deep, rapid breathing (Kussmaul). They may appear dehydrated, tachycardic and confused.
Baseline labs guide therapy and identify complications. If a test is unavailable, clinical judgment and bedside assessment guide management.

t.b: Low potassium may worsen arrhythmias; high sodium indicates dehydration
Osmolality >320 mOsm/kg suggests significant fluid loss
Elevated creatinine may limit fluid choice

sections.p: Severe hypoglycaemia, hyperkalaemia, cerebral oedema, arrhythmias, and shock are life‑threatening complications that require immediate attention.

Treat the precipitating cause, rehydrate with isotonic saline, start continuous insulin infusion, and correct electrolytes, especially potassium. Monitor glucose, ketones, electrolytes and acid–base status closely.

t.b: Start 1–2 L over 1–2 h, then adjust based on urine output
Start 0.1 U/kg/h, adjust to keep glucose 200‑250 mg/dL

sections.p: After resolution, transition to subcutaneous insulin, educate on sick‑day rules, and monitor for hypoglycaemia. Regular follow‑up reduces recurrence.
Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) and lactic acidosis share hyperglycaemia but lack significant ketosis and have different fluid needs.
Serum ketones may be falsely low if the patient has been on insulin for a short period; urine ketones can be negative early in DKA.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe dehydration, altered consciousness, persistent vomiting, chest pain, severe abdominal pain, or any sign of shock

faq.q: Can DKA occur in type 2 diabetes?
faq.a: Yes, especially in new‑onset type 2 or in severe stress situations.

faq.q: What is the first step in treatment?
faq.a: Restore volume with isotonic saline before starting insulin.
Insulin drives potassium into cells, risking hypokalaemia and cardiac arrhythmias.
